Breathe the H

English /h/ is a real puff of breath. French has none, so we drop it, or we add it where it should not be. Three short steps to fix both.

The rule

/h/ is breath, not noise. Put your hand in front of your mouth: house, happy, behind: you feel air. Two French traps:

① Dropping it: ’ouse, ’appy, ’ello. ② Adding it to words that start with a vowel: h‑eating, h‑engineer, h‑upcycling.

WHO  ·  HOW  →  breathe the H
WHAT · WHERE · WHEN · WHY · WHICH → no H, just /w/

Careful pair: who/whose/whole = /h/ (the w is silent), but what/where/when = /w/ (the h is silent). Same wh-, opposite sound.

Two more places the h goes quiet:

③ After <g> and <r>: ghost, rhinoceros, and the one that matters here, rheostat (REE-o-stat, not ré-o-stat). ④ The <xh> words: the h is silent and the x turns into a GZ sound: exhaust eg-ZAWST, exhausted, exhibit eg-ZIB-it.

More exceptions: honour(able), honest(ly), heir(ess), hour (and its family), exhausted, vehicle, exhibit, shepherd.

1 · Sort the word

Decide how the word sounds. You will see why after each one.

2 · Minimal pairs

Same word, one letter of breath apart. Say each pair aloud; feel the H switch on. Tap a word to hear it.

3 · Say it

Read aloud, slowly, with the breath on every bold H. Then at speed.

Who has Hugo’s helmet? How heavy is it?
How happy Harry held his heavy hammer.
Now no breath: What, where, when, why: just /w/. Eat, engineer, energy, upcycling: start on the vowel, no h.
Breathe the H.
The letter h is breath, not noise.
WHO and HOW both breathe the H.
WHAT · WHERE · WHEN · WHY · WHICH have no H, just the letter W.
With who, whose, whole, the letter W, but with what, where, when, the letter H is silent.
